Leaving the market is only the first decision: test the rule for getting back in

Four interactive charts compare regular investing with a stated exit and re-entry rule across fast rebounds, longer declines and whipsaws, counting the same deposits and all waiting cash.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 8 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Write an exit rule and a return-to-market rule before seeing the outcome

Interactive planning lab

Remain invested: ending total resources$18,401.05
Timing rule: ending investment plus cash$16,415.18
Timing rule minus remain invested-$1,985.87

Twelve authored hypothetical monthly total returns; no historical index, financial crisis replay, forecast or probability. Selected path: Fast rebound. Returns are treated as already net of ongoing fund expenses, with income reinvested. Both strategies start with the same capital and receive the same month-end new cash. The timing rule makes at most one exit and one re-entry: after the current return and deposit, exit on the entered drawdown from the observed index peak; while out, earn the entered cash interest and re-enter at a later close when the index reaches the entered rise from the exit close. It participates in market returns again only in the next month. Exit month: 2; re-entry month: 3. Proportional trade costs are deducted at each switch; initial implementation and final liquidation costs are excluded for both. Cash is included even if re-entry never happens. Taxes, inflation, settlement delays and interest-rate changes are excluded. This monthly-close rule is not a stop order or a recommendation.

The central idea

A timing strategy needs an exit, a re-entry and a fair accounting of cash, costs and contributions. Test the rule on paths where it helps and paths where it hurts before confusing hindsight with a plan.

01

“I will wait until things look safer” needs an operational meaning

When markets are falling, selling can feel like completing a decision. In practice it opens another one: when will the money return to the investment? A person can correctly identify a worrying economy and still re-enter at an unattractive price, or stay in cash as a rebound begins.

FINRA’s explanation of market timing identifies transaction costs and the possibility of missing recovery during volatile periods. It also recognizes that timing attempts can sometimes improve returns. This article examines that tradeoff without assuming every market timer fails or that remaining invested avoids losses.

The relevant planning question is whether an investor has a rule that can be followed with information available at the time. “Buy at the bottom” cannot be executed as written, because a bottom becomes identifiable only after subsequent prices are known.

The tool makes one particular rule explicit so its consequences can be inspected. It is a teaching example, not an optimized investment system or an instruction to place a stop order. A different observation frequency or execution price could produce different results.

02

Specify the sequence of events before running the comparison

Both strategies begin with the same invested capital. Each month the market return arrives first. Both then receive the same new cash, representing money becoming available at that month-end. The remain-invested strategy puts that cash into the investment immediately.

The timing strategy observes the total-return index at the close. If its drawdown from the highest index level observed so far reaches the entered exit threshold, the strategy sells at that close and deducts the proportional switching cost. It therefore experiences the decline that triggered the decision; it does not escape a loss already observed.

While out, its entire balance earns the assumed cash interest, converted from an effective annual rate to a monthly factor. New monthly savings join that cash. At a later close, if the index has risen by the entered percentage from the exit close, the strategy buys again and pays the switching cost.

Market participation resumes in the following month. The rebound that triggered re-entry occurred while this strategy was still in cash. Even a zero-percent re-entry threshold requires a later observation; the code cannot sell and buy back in the same decision step.

There is at most one exit and one re-entry in this model. It does not simulate an endlessly repeated trading strategy. If no exit is triggered, the strategies remain identical. If re-entry never occurs, the cash is still counted in ending resources.

03

Include uncomfortable paths for both choices

The first chart isolates the selected market index, starting at 100, without household contributions. The table below discloses all twelve authored monthly returns before applying the scale control.

The fast-rebound path places large gains soon after two losses. The longer-decline path continues falling before a partial recovery. The whipsaw path alternates meaningful losses and gains. The labels describe these authored shapes, not categories with estimated real-world probabilities.

The grouped ending-value chart runs the same selected rule across all three. With default inputs, the rule falls behind remaining invested on the fast rebound but finishes ahead on the longer decline. Both results matter. Selecting only the first would conceal the benefit of being out during further losses; selecting only the second would conceal the cost of missing an early rebound.

These are not a representative sample, and averaging their outcomes would not establish an expected return. Historical research would require a defensible dataset, a rule fixed before evaluation, consistent execution assumptions and checks on data mining. Three illustrative stories cannot provide that evidence.

04

Count every dollar, including the money waiting outside the fund

The second chart compares total resources. The timing line includes the investment whenever invested and the full cash balance whenever waiting. There is no hidden disappearance of sale proceeds, and the remain-invested line receives exactly the same contributions on exactly the same dates.

The dashed line records cumulative capital supplied by the household. At the default CAD 10,000 start and CAD 500 per month, both strategies receive CAD 16,000 by month twelve. A balance above the original CAD 10,000 does not by itself establish an investment gain, because CAD 6,000 more has been added.

Month one illustrates the order. A 12% loss reduces CAD 10,000 to CAD 8,800; the CAD 500 deposit then raises it to CAD 9,300. The 20% exit threshold has not yet been reached. In month two, another 12% decline leaves CAD 8,184 before the next deposit, or CAD 8,684 afterward. The index is now 22.56% below its initial peak, triggering the default exit and its CAD 8.684 switching cost.

The strategy cannot retroactively sell at CAD 10,000, exclude the two triggering losses or invest next month’s pay before it was earned. These small accounting choices can change the apparent success of a timing story much more than a polished chart suggests.

05

Give dollar-cost averaging a specific job

Dollar-cost averaging means investing equal amounts at regular intervals. Investor.gov explains that the same cash buys more units at a lower price and fewer at a higher price. That is a purchase mechanism, not a guarantee of profit.

The regular-contribution benchmark here invests new cash as it becomes available. FINRA distinguishes this from deliberately staging money already available, where part of an existing lump sum waits in cash. Those are different funding situations. This comparison does not give either strategy twelve future paycheques on day one.

A standing schedule can reduce the need to choose a fresh purchase date every month. It does not choose a suitable fund, eliminate concentration or ensure that a fund’s eventual sale price exceeds the investor’s cost. The unit-cost article shows why a lower average purchase cost can coexist with an investment loss.

Keep the schedule affordable. If a job loss interrupts income, reassess the saving amount and reserve needs. Reducing contributions because cash is needed for essentials is a household funding decision; it is different from predicting a market bottom. A long-term plan must accommodate that distinction.

06

Treat the return-to-market threshold as seriously as the exit threshold

The matrix changes both decisions. Its rows replace the exit drawdown; its columns replace the rise required from the exit close before re-entry. Each cell shows the timing rule’s ending resources minus the remain-invested strategy under the selected path.

A positive cell means this rule finishes ahead in that illustration, including its waiting cash and modeled switching costs. A negative cell means it finishes behind. A zero can mean no exit was triggered, rather than that timing was perfectly executed.

Finding the best cell after seeing every monthly return is hindsight. A person implementing the rule would need to choose those settings before knowing which path arrived. The matrix is useful because it shows sensitivity, not because its most attractive number supplies a reliable future setting.

The model deliberately avoids a “miss the best days” calculation that removes favorable returns without stating how an investor would have identified those days in advance. It also retains avoided negative periods when the rule is in cash. A fair comparison needs the whole feasible path.

07

Address crash anxiety with a written response plan

For someone worried about a financial-crisis-style event, start with what a loss would prevent them from doing. Map spending deadlines and access to reserves, then inspect the dollar stress in the balanced-fund companion. Holding a diversified fund does not make money needed next month safe from price changes.

If the allocation exceeds the investor’s capacity or willingness to take losses, revising it can be sensible. That is a decision about the household’s needs. It does not require pretending to know the next turning point. A portfolio chosen only because it performed well recently may need reassessment even before another crash occurs.

Write down the regular contribution amount, the conditions for a planning review and any rebalancing approach. If a timing strategy is still being considered, document both decisions, cash treatment, costs and execution assumptions. Include a plan for never reaching the hoped-for re-entry price.

This illustration omits tax, inflation, settlement delays and changing cash rates. It uses no special Canadian capital-gains rate and imports no US holding-period tax rule from the FINRA source. Those omitted effects need separate analysis before a real transaction. The practical lesson is a complete decision process with honest tradeoffs, rather than certainty about what the market will do next.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Three deliberately authored twelve-month return paths, not historical market data, a backtest, probability estimates or a forecast. These examples do not prove either strategy always wins.
